# Boundary to interior: predicting volume fields from the surface {#sec-interior}

**On the one task that asks for the flow rather than the wall pressure,
how an architecture treats an interior point decides the result. Let the
interior queries interact as tokens and give them the signed distance to
the wall, the input GeoTransolver's volume configuration receives, and
ISLA at a third of the parameters, on the frame-free reference frame, is
27% more accurate than that configuration on interior velocity (0.078
against 0.107, float32), 7% less accurate on interior pressure (0.055
against 0.051) and 14% less accurate on eddy viscosity (0.100 against 0.088,
on the recipe's normalized viscosity metric; @sec-nb-relint-verdict). The
similarity-gauge interior configuration behind the rest of this chapter's
numbers, now the prior configuration, stood at 27%, 6% and 27% (0.080,
0.055 and 0.112); in bfloat16 its pressure ordering read the other way (0.057 against
0.062), because bfloat16 inflates GeoTransolver-volume's errors by 20–23% and
ISLA's by 4–7% (@sec-nb-fp32-interior-regrade); decode
the queries passively, so that a prediction at one point never depends on
which other points are asked for, and ISLA is 3.1x behind on pressure
(float32; 2.6x in bfloat16).**
That passive contract is worth keeping for a surrogate queried on
arbitrary probe sets, and on DrivAerML the complete passive configuration
as built (a separate four-block read decoder, no signed-distance input)
costs 3.1x in interior pressure error in float32; what query independence alone would
cost, at matched decoder depth and inputs, is not yet measured. The
interacting configuration's advantage is tied to its training query count:
on the trained query-token model the pressure error at fixed points is 0.062
when 10,000 points are queried together, 0.077 at 2,000 and 0.110 at 1,000,
against 0.056 at 40,000 (@sec-interior-companion). The passive
deficit ratio is smallest at the wall and grows with distance from it, but
almost all of the excess squared error on the sampled points (95%) lies
within the first 5 cm of the wall, so the ratio's growth does not by itself
name a missing mechanism (@sec-interior-distance).
Two attempts to supply interior context without breaking the contract fail:
off-surface
latent tokens along anchor normals make ISLA worse, and the exact-kernel
MeshTransformer's boundary-integral decoder is 8x behind (0.76M parameters
against 27.6M) because potential flow is the wrong prior for a separated
wake. Interaction among the queries narrows the gap: the query-token
configuration takes pressure from 3.1x to 1.19x behind in float32 (1.03x in
bfloat16) and leaves velocity (1.28x) and eddy viscosity (1.61x) behind, the
two fields most tied to wall distance; adding the signed distance as a query input, so that the two
models see the same inputs, moves ISLA to 0.91x on pressure and 0.64x on
velocity in bfloat16 and halves the eddy-viscosity deficit (1.29x); in
float32 the same two checkpoints stand at 1.06x, 0.73x and 1.27x (three
seeds: 1.08x, 0.75x and 1.27x, @sec-nb-qtsdf-seed44), so the pressure lead
was a bfloat16 artifact and the velocity lead is real.

## The task {#sec-interior-task}

A surrogate that returns only wall pressure answers one engineering
question (forces); one that returns the volume flow answers the rest
(wake structure, cooling-flow paths, where separation begins). The task
here is the second, in its strictest form: predict the fields inside the
fluid domain from the vehicle surface alone. ISLA is held to that form.
GeoTransolver's volume configuration is not: it never sees the surface
sample, and takes instead, at every interior point, the signed distance to
the full-resolution vehicle surface and its gradient (the *Resources*
paragraph below), which is the surface information in a different, denser
form.

**Data.** DrivAerML (@sec-datasets), the 435-car training split and the
48-car validation split used for every DrivAerML comparison in this book.
Each car contributes a sample of the vehicle boundary (cell centroids,
unit normals, cell areas as measure weights) and 10,000 interior query
points sampled from the CFD volume mesh. The boundary sample is not the
10,000 cells the recipe names: the volume dataset applies both a
10,000-cell and a 10,000-point subsample to every boundary, cells first,
and the point cut keeps only the cells whose three vertices all survive, so
about 365 cells per car (341–395 on four validation cars) reach every ISLA
configuration in this chapter; GeoTransolver's volume configuration reads
no boundary and is unaffected (verified in the reader code and by running
the pipeline; results/isla_qt_companion_dependence_2026-09-08.json). Every ISLA number in
this chapter is therefore a result with roughly 365 surface tokens. The
rerun of the query-token configuration with the signed distance and the
intended 10,000 cells changes nothing: pressure 0.0572 against 0.0567,
velocity 0.0848 against 0.0853, eddy viscosity 0.1187 against 0.1215, all
within the preregistered 3% null band (@sec-nb-v0surf-verdict;
results/a35_v0_reduction_2026-09-09.json). On this task the interior
result is carried by the interacting queries and the signed distance, and
27x more surface information adds nothing measurable. The volume mesh
holds 150–166 million points per car, so the query sample covers roughly
6 × 10⁻⁵ of it, and it is overwhelmingly near-wall (median distance to
the surface 5 mm; @sec-interior-distance returns to this). Targets at
each query point are the static pressure, the three velocity components,
and the turbulent eddy viscosity ν_t. The interior sample is bit-identical
across every trained run.

**Metric.** For one car and one field f, the relative L2 error is

$$
\varepsilon = \frac{\lVert \hat f - f \rVert_2}{\lVert f \rVert_2}
$$

over the 10,000 interior sample points, where f is the field in training
normalisation: pressure as the coefficient C_p = (p − p_∞)/q_∞ with
p_∞ = 0, velocity as U/|U_∞| with the freestream mean included, Frobenius
norm over the three components, and eddy viscosity as the standardized
(ν_t − 4.8×10⁻⁴)/9.4×10⁻⁴, scored *before* inverse normalization. The
viscosity denominator is therefore the norm of a mean-subtracted field, and
an eddy-viscosity value of 0.122 is not a 12.2% error in physical ν_t;
orderings between arms under this frozen metric stand, but a ratio of
arithmetic means need not survive a different centering. The number reported for an arm is the
arithmetic mean of ε over the 48 validation cars; where a table cell is a
ratio, the numerator is the named arm and the denominator is
GeoTransolver on the same 48 cars, so a ratio above 1 means the arm is
less accurate than GeoTransolver. This is the reverse of the convention
in the rest of the book, where ratios are baseline ÷ ISLA and a value
above 1 favours ISLA; it is used here because GeoTransolver is the most
accurate arm on this task. Velocity's denominator includes the
freestream and is never small; pressure is a gauge quantity whose
denominator can be tiny far from the body (@sec-interior-distance).

**Protocol.** 500 epochs, learning rate 1e-3 for every arm (no per-arm
tuning on this task), bf16, no augmentation, two seeds (42 and 43).

**Resources and inputs.** The arms are not resource-matched, and they do
not see the same inputs; both facts are read from each lane's training
log and configuration
(results/v0_interior_resources_2026-09-07.json). Every memory figure in this
chapter is the training logger's peak `torch.cuda.memory_reserved()`, one
instrument for all arms here but a different one from the allocated-memory
figures of @sec-mt2-cost. GeoTransolver's volume
configuration has **27.6M parameters** and peaks at **8.8 GB** per GPU: it is
the surface configuration's 12-layer, 256-wide backbone (@sec-baselines)
plus local ball-query features at six radii from 0.01 to 5.0
nondimensional units, which the surface configuration does not use. Its
tokens are the **10,000 interior points only**; the boundary surface sample
is not consumed. Each interior token carries its coordinates, the signed
distance to the full-resolution vehicle surface and that distance's
gradient (the unit normal of the nearest wall), and the freestream
velocity enters globally; the geometry encoder runs on the interior point
cloud. ISLA in its passive-decode configuration has **9.9M parameters**
(8.9M in the surface configuration, @sec-mt2, plus four read blocks) and
peaks at **4.9 GB**; it consumes the surface tokens (about 365 cells, see
*Data*) with normals and areas, the freestream direction, and at each interior query its
position and, in the SDF-gradient arm, the same wall normal GeoTransolver
receives, but not the distance itself. The latent-volume-token arm has
10.0M parameters at 5.8 GB; the exact-kernel MeshTransformer 0.76M at
4.0 GB. Per-step times at this size are 0.04–0.05 s for every arm except
the query-token configuration (0.28 s; its per-slice geometry spans all
20,000 tokens). With the exact activation recompute and the compiled
geometry region of @sec-mt2-cost, the query-token configuration's peak
memory falls from 6.3 to 2.5 GiB at 0.83x the step time
(results/isla_qt_cost_2026-09-07.json), so it matches GeoTransolver-volume's
interior pressure at a third of the parameters and, indicatively, under a
third of the memory (the 2.5 GiB is allocated memory on one GPU and the
8.8 GB reserved memory from a training run; the lanes that produced the
interior numbers ran the stored path at 6.0 GB reserved), while remaining
about five times slower per training step. Three
differences therefore separate GeoTransolver from ISLA's passive decode
on this task: interaction among the query tokens, the signed-distance
input, and 2.8x the parameters with local features. The chapter's
headline ratio bounds the price of ISLA's contracts as ISLA is built; the
query-token arm isolates the first difference between GeoTransolver and
ISLA, though not between ISLA's two interior configurations, which also
differ in decoder depth (@sec-interior-results). GeoTransolver-volume's
freestream input is the physical velocity (38.9 m/s) where ISLA's is the
unit direction, the asymmetry that produced the baselines' HiLiftAeroML
deficit; retrained with the unit direction it changes by under 2% on every
field (0.0617 / 0.131 / 0.0936 against 0.0620 / 0.1334 / 0.0939;
@sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict), so every ratio in this chapter stands against
either version of the baseline.

### Query independence as a first-class property {#sec-interior-query-independence}

In ISLA's passive configuration an interior query is never a token. The
encoder sees the surface only; interior queries are decoded passively, by read blocks
(@sec-mt2-forward) that read the slice states and the boundary tokens
and write nothing back, so a prediction at one interior point is
independent of the other interior points queried (verified in fp64 to
10⁻¹², @sec-query-independence). This is a property of the interior
decode: ISLA's surface predictions in this book come from a configuration
whose heads read the interacting encoder tokens, and do not share it. A
user who asks for one streamline, a plane, or the whole domain gets the
same answer at every shared point, at a cost linear in the points asked
for. GeoTransolver's queries are tokens, so its answer at a point depends
on the other points requested with it.

The passive route was tested at matched depth and inputs by the companion
program: a decode that reads through twelve blocks from an interacting
support set of 5,000 surface tokens carrying the signed distance, with 5,000
passive queries, scores 0.078 / 0.107 / 0.269 (pressure, velocity, eddy
viscosity; two seeds, float32) against 0.055 / 0.080 / 0.112 for the
interacting query-token configuration, 1.43x, 1.34x and 2.41x, past the
preregistered pressure falsifier of 0.060. Twelve read blocks against four
buy 13% on pressure and the support set 12%; neither moves eddy viscosity.
The interacting queries therefore provide computation at the requested points
through every encoder layer rather than geometric context, the passive route
is closed for ISLA at matched depth
(`research/transfer_program/studies/computational_support/d1_verdict_2026-09-10.json`, companion #sec-computational-support).
Whether the request-size dependence is then a training question was tested
directly: the same configuration trained with the interior request size
drawn per sample between 2,000 and 20,000 points (@sec-nb-qcount-prereg)
reduces the dependence by about 40% (the 2,000-request penalty on pressure
falls from +38% to +24%, on velocity from +59% to +31%, on eddy viscosity
from +49% to +31%, and the 2,000-request prediction itself improves from
0.0753 to 0.0703) at a 3.7% accuracy cost at the training count (0.0567
against 0.0547), and converges upward at 20,000 as before. The dependence
is therefore partly a training-distribution artifact and partly intrinsic to
the interacting decode, so query-count consistency is an architectural
question after all, with count augmentation as a partial and costly
mitigation (`results/qcount_reduction_2026-09-11.json`, @sec-nb-qcount-verdict).

### How each architecture treats an interior point

*GeoTransolver.* The interior points are the tokens. Each carries its
coordinates, the signed distance to the wall and the wall normal at the
nearest surface point; the tokens are routed to slices and attend through
the same layers as in the surface task, so an interior token gathers
context from the other interior tokens before it is decoded, and its
knowledge of the geometry comes from the signed-distance inputs and from
ball-query features over neighbouring interior points at six radii, not
from surface tokens, which this configuration does not receive.

*ISLA.* The passive decoder builds every query-side invariant from the
query position q, the freestream direction d, and a unit normal n̂ at
the query. Lengths need two conventions kept apart. The recipe stores
coordinates nondimensionalized by the dataset's per-case reference
length L_ref, which is 5 m for every DrivAerML car; ISLA then measures q
from the centroid in *gauge units*, dividing by its constant gauge of
8.0 in those nondimensional units (40 m physical on DrivAerML). The
invariants are
{|q|, log|q|, q̂·d, q̂·n̂, n̂·d}. Surface points have normals; interior
points do not, so a normal has to be constructed. Two constructions are
measured.

The first is a *soft-assigned proxy normal*. Each slice s of the encoder
has an equivariant anchor: a measure-weighted mean position z_s and a
mean normal m_s. The query is softly assigned to anchors by distance and
inherits their normals,

$$
\hat n(q) = \operatorname{normalize}\!\Big(\sum_s a_s(q)\, m_s\Big),
\qquad
a_s(q) = \operatorname{softmax}_s\!\big(-|q - z_s|^2 / \rho^2\big),
$$

with ρ = 0.25 gauge units (2.0 nondimensional units, 10 m on
DrivAerML). It is exactly SE(3)-covariant, smooth,
defined everywhere and parameter-free; every read block and the vector
head run unchanged.

The second is the *signed-distance-field gradient*: the data pipeline
computes, for every interior point, the distance to the full-resolution
vehicle surface and its gradient, which is the unit normal of the nearest
wall. Passed as the query normal it overrides the proxy; it is equally
covariant and carries information about the local wall geometry that the
proxy does not.

*The exact-kernel MeshTransformer, an earlier design of this program.*
A one-layer attention encoder reads the boundary sample; its decoder
then evaluates the exact double-layer and single-layer Laplace kernels
from every boundary panel to the query, weighted by learned,
operator-conditioned densities, so an interior prediction is a
discretized boundary integral rather than a learned interpolation. Its
contracts — similarity equivariance and, when declared, linearity in the
drive — are exact for potential flow, where these kernels are the
Green's-function representation of the solution, and the decoder is
query-independent by construction. The arm trained here drops the
surface-trace terms so that every interior output is the boundary
integral alone; its parameter count on this task is not recorded. The
rest of this chapter calls it the exact-kernel decoder.

### ISLA with query tokens {#sec-interior-query-tokens}

*ISLA, interacting mode.* The same architecture admits its interior
queries into the encoder as tokens. Each query is seeded with the five
invariants of its position, its wall normal (the SDF gradient) and the
freestream direction, exactly as a surface token is, plus a learned
type embedding, and enters the measure-weighted slice routing with a
learned weight relative to the surface measure; the twelve slice layers
then run over surface and query tokens together, and the heads read the
query tokens. Every invariant is a function of relative geometry, so the
prediction stays rotation- and translation-covariant by construction (and,
with the similarity gauge, scale-covariant; verified to roundoff in fp64,
@sec-mt2-contracts). What is given up is
query independence: a query's prediction now depends on the other queries
in the batch, as GeoTransolver's does, and, because each query's routing
weight is a learned multiple of the *geometric mean* of the source weights,
on how finely the surface is sampled and how many queries are asked for
(splitting every surface cell in two at half the area moves a small random
model's output by 4–9%, @sec-mt2-contracts); on the trained checkpoint the
dependence on the number of co-queried points is measured in
@sec-interior-companion. Nothing else changes: 8.9M
parameters, the surface configuration's hyperparameters, no signed-distance
input, no local features.

## Results {#sec-interior-results}

**With its interior queries admitted as interacting tokens and given the
signed distance to the wall, ISLA's reference configuration is 27% more
accurate than GeoTransolver's volume configuration on interior velocity
(0.078 against 0.107 in float32, a ratio of 0.73), 7% less accurate on
interior pressure (0.055 against 0.051, 1.07) and 14% less accurate on eddy
viscosity (0.100 against 0.088, 1.14), at a third of the parameters and with
the two models' inputs matched (@sec-nb-relint-verdict); the similarity-gauge
configuration that produced the diagnostics in this chapter, now the prior
configuration, stood at 0.73, 1.06 and 1.27 (0.080, 0.055 and 0.112); the bfloat16 numbers that follow in this section (0.057 against
0.062 on pressure, 0.91x) inflate GeoTransolver-volume's errors by 20–23%
and ISLA's by 4–7% (@sec-nb-fp32-interior-regrade), and every ratio in the
tables below is a bfloat16 ratio until its float32 re-evaluation lands; without the signed distance the
query tokens trail GeoTransolver-volume on every field (1.19 / 1.28 / 1.61
in float32; 1.03 on pressure in bfloat16); the passive, query-independent
decode is 3.1x behind in float32 (2.6x in bfloat16), and no passive
construction tried closes that gap.** @tbl-interior gives the
arithmetic-mean relative L2 over the 48 validation cars for each arm, both
seeds, and the ratio to GeoTransolver; @fig-interior-arms draws the
pressure column.

| arm | parameters | peak memory | pressure (seed 42 / 43) | velocity | ν_t | pressure ratio, arm ÷ GeoTransolver |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GeoTransolver-volume: interior points as interacting tokens with signed distance and wall normal as inputs; no surface tokens | 27.6M | 8.8 GB | 0.062 (0.0622 / 0.0618) | 0.133 | 0.094 | 1.0 |
| ISLA, query tokens + signed distance: interior queries as interacting tokens on the surface tokens' slice routing, with the SDF-gradient normal and the signed distance at the query | 8.9M | 6.0 GB | 0.057 (0.0569 / 0.0565) | 0.085 | 0.122 | 0.91 |
| ISLA, query tokens, SDF-gradient normal only; no signed-distance input | 8.9M | 6.0 GB | 0.064 (0.0636 / 0.0642) | 0.155 | 0.160 | 1.03 |
| ISLA, passive decode from 10,000 surface tokens, SDF-gradient normal at the query | 9.9M | 4.9 GB | 0.160 (0.166 / 0.153) | 0.308 | 0.372 | 2.6 |
| ISLA, passive decode, proxy normal | 9.9M | 4.9 GB | 0.193 (0.195 / 0.191) | 0.337 | 0.418 | 3.1 |
| ISLA + 769 latent volume tokens | 10.0M | 5.8 GB | 0.228 (0.233 / 0.224) | 0.371 | 0.581 | 3.7 |
| exact-kernel decoder, double-layer | 0.76M | 4.0 GB | 0.496 (0.499 / 0.492) | 0.549 | 0.727 | 8.0 |

: Interior relative L2 error on the 48 DrivAerML validation cars
(arithmetic mean over cars, then over two seeds; per-seed pressure in
parentheses), 10,000 interior queries per car (plus the surface tokens
for the ISLA and exact-kernel arms, about 365 cells per car rather than the
nominal 10,000; see *Data*), 500 epochs, learning rate 1e-3. Peak
memory is the training logger's reserved memory for every row (one
instrument within this table; not the allocated-memory instrument of
@sec-mt2-cost).
Ratio = arm ÷ GeoTransolver, so a value above 1 means less accurate than
GeoTransolver; this is the reverse of the book's usual baseline ÷ ISLA
convention. The arms are not resource-matched and do not receive the same
inputs (parameters and peak per-GPU training memory from each lane's log,
results/v0_interior_resources_2026-09-07.json; inputs in the *Resources
and inputs* paragraph of @sec-interior-task). Seed spreads are 1–8% of
the means, so every ratio is resolved. Sources:
`results/a35_v0_reduction_2026-09-08.json` (GeoTransolver, both query-token,
passive-decode and exact-kernel rows) and
`results/v0_lvt_reduction_2026-09-07.json` (the latent-volume-token row).
{#tbl-interior}

```{python}
#| label: fig-interior-arms
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Interior pressure error by architecture on the 48 DrivAerML validation
#|   cars. Bars are the two-seed mean of the per-car arithmetic-mean relative
#|   L2 error; the two dots on each bar are the individual seeds (filled =
#|   seed 42, open = seed 43, same x). Labels above the bars give the ratio to
#|   GeoTransolver (arm ÷ GeoTransolver; above 1 means less accurate than
#|   GeoTransolver). How to read this: it shows the pressure column of the
#|   table only; velocity and eddy viscosity rank the arms identically
#|   except for the two query-token arms (with the signed distance ISLA leads
#|   GeoTransolver on velocity, 0.64x, and trails on eddy viscosity, 1.29x;
#|   without it 1.16x and 1.71x), and are not drawn. Data:
#|   results/a35_v0_reduction_2026-09-08.json (six arms) and
#|   results/v0_lvt_reduction_2026-09-07.json (the latent-volume-token bar).
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
# book palette (mirrors figures.py without importing it: that module
# switches matplotlib to Agg, which suppresses inline output here)
BLUE, RED, PURPLE = "#2a78d6", "#e34948", "#7b4fb3"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})

red = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "a35_v0_reduction_2026-09-08.json"))["v0"]
lvt = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "v0_lvt_reduction_2026-09-07.json"))
LVT_PRESSURE = {s: lvt[f"v0_mt2_lvt_sdf_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)}
arms = [
    ("GeoTransolver-volume\ninterior points as tokens", lambda s: red[f"v0_gt_vol_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"], RED),
    ("ISLA, query tokens\n+ signed distance", lambda s: red[f"v0_isla_qtsdfval_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"], BLUE),
    ("ISLA, query tokens\nSDF-gradient normal", lambda s: red[f"v0_isla_qt_sdf_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"], BLUE),
    ("ISLA, passive decode\nSDF-gradient normal", lambda s: red[f"v0_mt2_int_sdf_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"], BLUE),
    ("ISLA, passive decode\nproxy normal", lambda s: red[f"v0_mt2_int_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"], BLUE),
    ("ISLA + 769 latent\nvolume tokens", lambda s: LVT_PRESSURE[s], BLUE),
    ("exact-kernel decoder\ndouble-layer", lambda s: red[f"v0_mt1k_vol_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"], PURPLE),
]
seeds = (42, 43)
means = [statistics.mean(get(s) for s in seeds) for _, get, _ in arms]
gt = means[0]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.8, 4.4))
x = range(len(arms))
ax.bar(x, means, width=0.58, color=[c for _, _, c in arms], alpha=0.85, zorder=2)
for i, (_, get, c) in enumerate(arms):
    ax.plot([i], [get(42)], marker="o", ms=6, mfc=INK, mec=INK, mew=1.0, ls="none", zorder=4)
    ax.plot([i], [get(43)], marker="o", ms=6, mfc="white", mec=INK, mew=1.0, ls="none", zorder=4)
    r = means[i] / gt
    ax.text(i, means[i] + 0.012, f"{means[i]:.3f}\n{r:.2f}x" if r < 1.5 else f"{means[i]:.3f}\n{r:.1f}x",
            ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax.set_xticks(list(x))
ax.set_xticklabels([n for n, _, _ in arms], fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("interior pressure rel-L2, mean over 48 cars [–]")
ax.set_ylim(0, max(means) * 1.25)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three things in the table carry the section. First, the query-token row:
the same ISLA, with its interior queries allowed to interact, comes within
1.19x of GeoTransolver-volume on pressure in float32 (1.03x in bfloat16,
seeds within 1%) and trails on velocity (1.28x) and eddy viscosity (1.61x). Second, the ordering of the two
passive constructions: the SDF-gradient normal beats the proxy normal by
1.2x on pressure and on every field, so a true wall normal at the query is
better information than a covariant blend of anchor normals. Third, the
size of what the passive decode leaves: even with the better normal it is
3.1x behind on pressure in float32 (2.6x in bfloat16; 2.3x on velocity and
4.0x on eddy viscosity in bfloat16), and
the query-token row shows that this remainder is interaction, not the
normal. The exact-kernel decoder at 8.0x is taken up in
@sec-interior-negatives.

The comparison is between each architecture's natural interior mode, not
a matched-mechanism ablation, and the two modes differ in three ways at
once (@sec-interior-task): GeoTransolver's interior tokens interact with
each other where ISLA's queries only read what the surface-centred slices
hold; GeoTransolver receives the signed distance to the wall at every
query where ISLA receives at most the wall normal; and GeoTransolver's
volume configuration has 2.8x the parameters, with local features ISLA
lacks. The 3.1x bounds the price of ISLA's contracts as ISLA is built; it
does not say which difference carries it. The first is measured directly
by the query-token row of @tbl-interior: ISLA with its interior queries
admitted as interacting tokens on the same slice routing as the surface
tokens (@sec-interior-query-tokens) reaches 0.064 interior pressure, a
ratio of 1.03 to GeoTransolver, with the same wall-normal input as the
passive arm and no signed-distance value. The complete interacting
configuration therefore accounts for essentially the whole pressure gap
without the signed-distance input or the 2.8x parameters. It does not
isolate interaction as such: the passive arm decodes its queries through a
separate four-block read decoder, while the query-token arm sends them
through the twelve encoder blocks with a token-type embedding and a routing
weight, so the two ISLA configurations differ in query depth and readout as
well as in whether queries write into the shared state, and the
signed-distance scalar is available only to the interacting one. A
comparison that holds query depth and readout fixed and disables only the
writes from queries into the shared state is the experiment that would
price query independence itself; it is not yet measured
(@sec-program-status). What the interacting configuration pays is measured
(@sec-interior-companion): its prediction at a point depends on how many
other points are queried with it. What
interaction does not close is velocity (1.28x) and eddy viscosity (1.61x),
the two fields most tied to distance from the wall, which is the second
difference. The row above it measures that difference: with the signed
distance added as a query input, pressure error falls 11% (to 0.91x
GeoTransolver), velocity 45% (to 0.64x) and eddy viscosity 24% (to 1.29x),
so the input is worth most on the distance-dominated fields, as expected.
Against its preregistered bar on pressure (a 15% fall to count as
"supported", 5% to count as falsified) the 11% is in the inconclusive
band; the secondary bar, closing to within 1.1x of GeoTransolver, is met
(@sec-nb-qt-sdf-verdict). The third difference, GeoTransolver's 2.8x
parameters and six-radius local features, is what it still has, and eddy
viscosity at 1.29x is the one field where that still shows.

## Dependence on the query cloud {#sec-interior-companion}

**The interacting configuration's answer at a point depends on how many
other points are asked for with it, and the dependence is large below the
training query count.** Because the queries are tokens that route through
the same slices as the surface, and because each query's routing weight is
tied to the source measure in a way that also scales with the query count
(@sec-interior-query-tokens), a prediction at one interior point is a
function of the whole request. The size of that effect on the trained
query-token + signed-distance checkpoint (seed 42) was measured on four
validation cars: 1,000 fixed sentinel points, drawn from the recipe's own
interior sample, are predicted alone, with 1,000 companions, with 9,000
(the training count of 10,000 queries), and with 39,000, in the recipe's
inference precision (bf16) and in fp32
(results/isla_qt_companion_dependence_2026-09-08.json). The readout is the
relative L2 change of the sentinel predictions against the training-count
run, and the error of the sentinel predictions against the truth.

| Queries in the request | Change of the sentinel prediction vs. 10,000 (pressure / ν_t / velocity) | Pressure error at the sentinels | ν_t error | Velocity error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 (sentinels alone) | 0.100 / 0.348 / 0.142 | 0.110 | 0.362 | 0.163 |
| 2,000 | 0.051 / 0.181 / 0.090 | 0.077 | 0.197 | 0.124 |
| 10,000 (training count) | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0.062 | 0.080 | 0.091 |
| 40,000 | 0.029 / 0.048 / 0.045 | 0.056 | 0.084 | 0.089 |
| Passive configuration, any count (fp32) | 0.000 / 0.000 / 0.000 | 0.188 | 0.400 | 0.345 |

: Companion-query dependence of the trained ISLA query-token + signed
distance model, bf16 inference, mean over four validation cars (run_112,
run_115, run_118, run_129); relative L2 in the recipe's normalized target
space. The passive configuration (SDF-gradient normal arm) is the control:
its predictions at the sentinels are identical to fp32 roundoff whatever
else is queried. Data:
results/isla_qt_companion_dependence_2026-09-08.json. {#tbl-interior-companion}

Read against the chapter's headline: the query-token model's pressure
advantage over GeoTransolver-volume is 0.005 in absolute relative L2 (0.057
against 0.062 over 48 cars). Querying 2,000 points instead of 10,000 costs
0.015 at the sentinels, three times that margin; querying 1,000 costs 0.048,
ten times. Querying 40,000 changes the prediction by 3% and improves it
slightly. So the advantage is real at the operating point the model was
trained at, and it is not a property of the model at arbitrary request
sizes: a surrogate built from this configuration must be queried in batches
of at least the training count, or trained over a range of counts, or use a
query-mass convention that does not scale with the count
(@sec-mt2-contracts; the trained checkpoints use the count-dependent one).
GeoTransolver's queries are tokens too and its dependence was not measured
here. Splitting the sentinels into two halves with the same 9,000 companions
(a natural chunking) changes the prediction by 0.4–0.7% in fp32; in bf16 the
change is 2–4%, most of it autocast numerics rather than structure. The
near-identity of the passive control (0.000 in fp32, under 1% in bf16 from
autocast alone) confirms that the harness measures the model and that query
independence, where the architecture promises it, holds on trained weights.

## Where the deficit lives {#sec-interior-distance}

**The passive decode's error *ratio* to GeoTransolver is smallest at the
wall and grows with distance from it; its *excess error* is almost entirely
at the wall.** The two readings are of the same numbers and neither
identifies a missing mechanism. Summing the per-band squared errors of the
passive SDF-normal arm and of GeoTransolver-volume over the 48 cars and two
seeds, 94.6% of ISLA's excess pressure squared error over GeoTransolver
and 93.7% of its excess velocity squared error fall in the first
wall-distance band (below 0.01 nondimensional, about 5 cm), and over 99%
within 2 m (results/v0_interior_excess_sse_2026-09-08.json, reduced from
the band artifact below); those are fractions of the error on the
near-wall-biased sample, not volume integrals, and the query-token
configurations have not been reduced this way. The far-field ratio growth is
real, and it is where a passive read of surface-centred slices has least
to go on, but the far bands carry a negligible share of the sampled error,
so "missing volumetric context" is a reading of the ratio panel, not a
measured cause. The interior sample is stratified by the unsigned distance from
each query to the full-resolution vehicle surface (the SDF magnitude),
into three bands fixed before the models were evaluated. The thresholds
are 0.4 and 4.0 in the recipe's nondimensional coordinates, which
DrivAerML's per-case reference length L_ref = 5 m (read from the
artifact by the figure code) converts to metres: *near* is less than 2 m
from the surface, *mid* 2–20 m, *far* beyond 20 m. In ISLA's gauge units
(the constant gauge 8.0, 40 m physical) the same thresholds are 0.05 and
0.5. The sampler's near-wall
bias makes the bands very unequal — 97.8% of points near, 2.0% mid,
0.12% far, so the far band holds 4–25 points per car. Within each band
the per-car relative L2 is computed over the band's points only and
averaged over cars; @fig-interior-bands plots each arm's ratio to
GeoTransolver, which the sampling bias does not distort.

```{python}
#| label: fig-interior-bands
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Interior error relative to GeoTransolver as a function of distance from
#|   the wall. For each band, the per-car relative L2 is computed over that
#|   band's points and averaged over the 48 cars; the line is the ratio of
#|   two-seed means (arm ÷ GeoTransolver) and the small markers are the
#|   paired per-seed ratios (filled = seed 42, open = seed 43, same x). Left,
#|   pressure; right, velocity including the freestream mean. Log axis. The
#|   hollow purple marker is the exact-kernel decoder's far-band pressure, whose
#|   output there is identically zero (see text); it is not evidence of
#|   accuracy. How to read this: a rising line means the arm loses more
#|   ground to GeoTransolver as queries move away from the body. It does not
#|   show absolute error, which for pressure in the far band is dominated by
#|   a near-zero denominator. Data: results/v0_sdf_band_2026-09-05.json.
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
BLUE, RED, PURPLE = "#2a78d6", "#e34948", "#7b4fb3"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})

band = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "v0_sdf_band_2026-09-05.json"))
scheme = "prereg_Lref8"
pa = band["per_arm"]["case_mean"]
bands = band["band_definitions"][scheme]["names"]
thr = band["band_definitions"][scheme]["sdf_thresholds_nondim"]
L_m = band["global_data_first_case"]["L_ref"][0]  # metres per nondimensional unit
frac = band["band_fractions"][scheme]
edges = [f"< {thr[0] * L_m:g} m", f"{thr[0] * L_m:g}–{thr[1] * L_m:g} m", f"≥ {thr[1] * L_m:g} m"]
def pct(f):
    return f"{100 * f:.2g}" if f < 0.01 else f"{100 * f:.1f}"
ticks = [f"{b}\n{e}\n{pct(frac[b]['case_mean'])}% of points" for b, e in zip(bands, edges)]
arms = [("ISLA, SDF-gradient normal", "mt2_int_sdf", BLUE, "-"),
        ("ISLA, proxy normal", "mt2_int", BLUE, "--"),
        ("exact-kernel decoder", "mt1k_vol", PURPLE, "-")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.2, 4.2), sharey=True)
import math
for ax, field, title in zip(axes, ("pressure", "velocity"), ("pressure $C_p$", "velocity $U/|U_\\infty|$")):
    labels = []
    for name, key, color, ls in arms:
        g = [pa["gt_vol"][scheme][b][field] for b in bands]
        a = [pa[key][scheme][b][field] for b in bands]
        ratio = [ai["mean"] / gi["mean"] for ai, gi in zip(a, g)]
        ax.plot(range(3), ratio, color=color, ls=ls, lw=1.8, zorder=3)
        for i, (ai, gi) in enumerate(zip(a, g)):
            artefact = key == "mt1k_vol" and field == "pressure" and bands[i] == "far"
            for s_idx, mfc in enumerate((color, "white")):  # filled = seed 42, open = seed 43
                r = ai["seeds"][s_idx] / gi["seeds"][s_idx]
                ax.plot([i], [r], marker="o", ms=5 if not artefact else 8, ls="none",
                        mfc=mfc if not artefact else "white", mec=color,
                        mew=1.2 if not artefact else 1.6, zorder=4)
        labels.append([math.log10(ratio[-1]), name, color])
    # direct labels at the far band, pushed apart on the log axis where they would collide
    labels.sort()
    for j in range(1, len(labels)):
        if labels[j][0] - labels[j - 1][0] < 0.075:
            labels[j][0] = labels[j - 1][0] + 0.075
    for ly, name, color in labels:
        ax.text(2.08, 10 ** ly, name, color=color, fontsize=8.5, va="center")
    ax.axhline(1.0, color=RED, lw=1.2, zorder=2)
    ax.text(-0.35, 1.0, "GeoTransolver", color=RED, fontsize=8.5, va="bottom")
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xticks(range(3))
    ax.set_xticklabels(ticks, fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.4, 3.3)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10, color=INK2, loc="left")
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axes[0].set_ylabel("rel-L2 ratio, arm ÷ GeoTransolver [–, log]")
axes[0].set_yticks([0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20])
axes[0].set_yticklabels(["0.5", "1", "2", "5", "10", "20"])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

For ISLA with the SDF-gradient normal the pressure ratio runs 2.5x near,
3.7x mid, 3.3x far; velocity runs 2.3x near, 4.7x mid, 5.4x far. The
proxy-normal construction has the same shape (3.1x → 3.3x → 3.0x on
pressure, 2.5x → 4.5x → 6.4x on velocity). The near-wall band, where a
local-detail deficit would show first, is ISLA's *best* band on every
field. The reading is mechanical: ISLA's slices and anchors are
surface-centred and its read blocks consult slice states and boundary
tokens, so a query 10 m into the wake has nothing off-surface to read.
GeoTransolver's interior tokens supply that context to each other.

Two cautions about the far band. It holds 573 points across the 48 cars,
so its ratios move by tens of percent between seeds (the SDF arm's far
velocity ratio is 6.4x on one seed and 4.4x on the other). And far-band
*pressure* relative L2 is a poor readout for every architecture,
GeoTransolver included: 20 m from a car the true C_p has an RMS of
0.0055, so GeoTransolver's absolute error of about 0.01 in C_p gives it a
far-band pressure relative L2 of 1.71 — worse than predicting zero —
while its far-band velocity error is 0.021 |U_∞|. The 1.71 is a
denominator two orders of magnitude below the near-wall one, not an
engineering failure; the velocity panel, whose denominator is the
freestream, is the well-conditioned view of the far field.

## What does not work {#sec-interior-negatives}

Two mechanisms were tested as ways to give ISLA interior context or an
interior prior without giving up query independence. Both fail, for
different reasons: the first adds tokens that hurt, the second starts
from a physical prior that is worse than a constant on this flow.

### Latent volume tokens along anchor normals

**Latent volume tokens along anchor normals make the passive decode
worse, by 1.43x on pressure.** The construction: before the encoder,
each of the 256 slices has a geometric anchor (weighted mean position
z_s, mean normal m_s, and an RMS radius ρ_s of the points it owns). Three
tokens are placed off each anchor at z_s + c ρ_s m_s for c ∈ {0.5, 1, 2},
plus one at the centroid: 769 tokens whose positions are built
covariantly from the surface alone. They enter the slice routing as
interacting tokens with a separately learned measure weight and are
readable by interior queries through the ordinary read blocks; SE(3)
covariance and interior query independence survive. With the
SDF-gradient normal as base, the
result on the 48 cars is pressure 0.228 against 0.160 without the tokens
(0.233 / 0.224 against 0.166 / 0.153 by seed), velocity 0.371 against
0.308, eddy viscosity 0.581 against 0.372. The tokens did not fail to
help; they hurt, on both seeds. The likeliest reasons sit in the
construction: 769 near-body tokens with nearly identical invariant seeds
enter the measure-weighted routing on which the surface tokens rely, and
offsets of 0.5–2 anchor radii never reach the mid and far bands where
the deficit is largest. The supported statement is narrow:
**off-surface latent tokens placed along anchor normals, as interacting
tokens in ISLA's routing, degrade the interior decode.** It does not show
that interaction at the query itself is the only remedy.

### Why not an exact boundary-integral prior?

**The exact double-layer kernel is not a usable prior for separated
flow, so the flagship does not evaluate exact boundary-integral
kernels.** The question deserved asking: a boundary-integral decoder is
query-independent and exactly covariant by construction, and on linear
problems with exact labels the same decoder generalizes exactly across
boundary-condition content, which is why it was a candidate here; those
results are archived with the design. Three measurements on DrivAerML
answer it. The first is a zero-parameter
oracle: on the 45 of 48 validation cars whose remesh passes a
watertightness and Gauss-identity check, exact inviscid potential flow —
single- and double-layer integrals on the closed remesh, Neumann data
U_∞·n, second-kind solve, Bernoulli C_p — is evaluated at the recipe's
surface points and compared to the CFD pressure. Its measure-weighted
relative L2 is **4.8** (median 1.97, every car above 1.6); on the same
points, predicting C_p = 0 scores 1.00 and predicting each car's mean
C_p scores **0.77**. No numerical control rescues it (an oracle-optimal
affine rescale reaches 0.73; a remesh-resolution sweep is flat; the
solver is exact on a sphere to 0.07%). The physics is the reason: 69% of
a DrivAerML surface carries C_p in [−0.5, 0], the separated-base deficit,
where inviscid flow predicts roughly 0 to +0.13, and inviscid suction
peaks are two to three times too strong. A decoder built as "exact
Laplace kernel plus learned correction" starts from a field worse than a
constant.

The second is the trained exact-kernel decoder in @tbl-interior, at
**8.0x** GeoTransolver on interior pressure with learned densities on
top of the exact kernels. The comparison is not resource-matched: the
decoder's parameter count on this task was not recorded and peak
training memory was logged only as the 4–9 GB range across arms. The
caveat would matter if more capacity could plausibly close the gap; the
oracle says otherwise, because the field the learned densities must
correct is already worse than a constant.

The third is the decoder's far-band behaviour in @fig-interior-bands. Its
far-band pressure ratio of 0.59x GeoTransolver is not accuracy: its
far-field pressure output has decayed to identically zero (|C_p| below
10⁻⁶ on every far point, against a true RMS of 0.0055), which yields the
trivial relative L2 of 1.000 on all 48 cars and both seeds and beats
GeoTransolver's 1.71 only through the denominator problem above. On
far-band velocity, the well-conditioned readout, the exact-kernel
decoder is **16.7x** GeoTransolver (RMS velocity error 0.34 |U_∞|
against 0.027), and there is no distance band under any definition in
which the double-layer decoder is within 1.5x of GeoTransolver on
velocity. The exact-kernel line is closed for separated
three-dimensional aerodynamics on every readout in this book.

## Standing and open designs {#sec-interior-open}

**One architecture covers the surface and the interior, and on the interior
it leads on one field of three. ISLA with query tokens and the signed
distance as an input is 25% more accurate than GeoTransolver's volume
configuration on interior velocity (0.75x in float32, three seeds) at 8.9M parameters and
6.0 GB against 27.6M and 8.8 GB, with the two models' inputs matched, keeps
exact SE(3) covariance, and trails on pressure (1.08x) and eddy viscosity
(1.27x). At matched parameter count the ordering changes: the same ISLA
configuration at hidden width 344 (27.6M parameters, GeoTransolver-volume's
budget; exact recompute, two seeds, float32) scores 0.0497 / 0.0729 / 0.1033,
leading GeoTransolver-volume on pressure by 3% (0.97x) and on velocity by
32% (0.68x) and trailing on eddy viscosity by 18% (1.18x, inside the
preregistered inconclusive band 1.10–1.25). The float32 interior-pressure
ordering is therefore a parameter-budget statement, behind at 15M and ahead
at 27.6M, and width buys 9% / 8% / 7% for 1.8x parameters at about 1.3x step
time; the eddy-viscosity gap that remains is carried neither by width nor by
GeoTransolver-volume's local features (`research/transfer_program/studies/computational_support/campaign_d_verdict_2026-09-10.json`,
companion chapter 7 #sec-campaigns-interior). Where that gap lives is now
known. Splitting the saved float32 predictions by signed distance to the
wall, the two matched-parameter models are equal on eddy viscosity in the
near-wall band (signed distance below 0.01 body lengths, 77% of the points:
0.081 against 0.080), ISLA leads in the mid band (0.062 against 0.077) and
trails only in the far field (at or beyond 0.05 body lengths, 10% of the
points: 0.093 against 0.068), which carries 46% of ISLA's squared
eddy-viscosity error against 36% of GeoTransolver-volume's. Pressure and
velocity show the same pattern: near the wall ISLA leads on both (0.049
against 0.051; 0.086 against 0.128), far from it GeoTransolver-volume leads
(0.082 against 0.067; 0.040 against 0.033). The near-wall closure reading
(the modeled viscosity's wall-distance scaling) is refuted; the deficit is
the outer wake, where every surface anchor looks alike from a distant query
and the anchor-relative invariants lose the resolution a per-point network
on raw position keeps, and width helped that band least (0.101 to 0.093;
`research/transfer_program/studies/computational_support/band_decomposition_2026-09-10.json`). The
principled remedy that suggested, anchors organized by the flow rather than
the surface, was tested and falsified: three interacting wake tokens on the
drive axis (over the rear deck, in the near wake and 0.7 body lengths behind
the car) close a fifth of the far-band eddy-viscosity gap (0.093 to 0.087
against GeoTransolver-volume's 0.068; the two wake seeds agree to 1% while
the reference's differ by 14%, so the gain is within the reference's seed
spread), and the latent-volume tokens (anchors offset along the surface
normals) make the far band worse (0.110); neither moves the near-wall or
mid band or far-band pressure and velocity, and the wake tokens cost
nothing in time or memory (`research/transfer_program/studies/computational_support/band_decomposition_wake_2026-09-10.json`,
companion #sec-campaigns-interior). Two diagnostics on the saved
predictions then closed the anchor-geometry class of explanations. Split by
distance shell, the matched-parameter ISLA leads GeoTransolver-volume on
eddy viscosity everywhere within 0.4 body lengths of the surface (0.047
against 0.067 at 0.05–0.1 L, 0.042 against 0.053 at 0.1–0.2 L, parity at
0.2–0.4 L), around the car (0.034 against 0.050) and upstream (0.046 against
0.108); the entire deficit is the far wake beyond 0.4 body lengths
downstream, 2.2% of the query points (0.108 against 0.071; downstream region
0.102 against 0.070), worst beside the car. Pressure carries a uniform
15–25% deficit in every far shell that does not grow with distance and holds
under 2% of the squared error. A routing-mass probe over all twelve blocks
showed the premise behind the anchor reading to be false: interior query
tokens dominate 224–256 of the 256 slices in every layer, so 48–86% of the
anchors already sit off the surface, and they follow the query mass, which
is why few reach a wake that holds 2% of the sample; the wake tokens did
take routing mass (up to 53 slices) and did move anchors into the far wake,
and the far-wake error improved 6% for it (`research/transfer_program/studies/computational_support/far_field_shells_2026-09-10.json`).
The last sampling explanation was then tested and closed: the far wake
might be under-sampled at training time, so a measure-consistent
oversampling of the far field (inclusion probability rising with the signed
distance, exact importance weights recorded, the same construction as the
density probes; far band raised from 10% to 32% of the training queries)
was trained on two seeds and scored in float32 on the standard uniform
sample. It made every field worse in every band: far-shell eddy viscosity
0.193 against the reference's 0.118, recipe pressure +36%, velocity +22%,
eddy viscosity +48% (@sec-nb-farwake-verdict;
`results/farwake_far_field_shells_2026-09-11.json`). The arm trains the
interacting decode on one query distribution and scores it on another, so
part of that cost is a query-distribution swap penalty
(@sec-interior-companion) and the arm cannot separate "not under-sampled"
from "swamped by the swap"; what it settles is that a training-time
sampling law is not a deployable remedy. The remaining candidate is
representational (the downstream coordinate enters the seed only implicitly)
and is not scheduled. The sharper interior statement
is therefore: at matched parameters ISLA leads GeoTransolver-volume on
pressure, velocity and eddy viscosity everywhere except the far wake beyond
0.4 body lengths, which carries the whole 18% eddy-viscosity deficit. A
single-car training test locates each standing: with one car presented as
64 resampled views, ISLA's velocity lead over GeoTransolver-volume is
unchanged (0.67 against 0.65 at full data) and is therefore capacity, its
eddy-viscosity deficit widens (1.64 against 1.30) and is capacity too, and
its full-data pressure lead reverses on one car (1.25 against 0.92), so
that lead is generalization across cars rather than representation
(@sec-nb-overfit-interior). ISLA's
passive decode is the configuration to use when
interior query independence is contractual, at 9.9M parameters, 4.9 GB
and a 3.1x price in interior pressure error on DrivAerML (float32).** The parity is
mostly a full-data statement. Without the signed distance, trained on 54 or
109 cars, GeoTransolver-volume leads the query-token configuration by a
constant 1.2x on interior pressure (0.104 against 0.126 at 54 cars, 0.078
against 0.094 at 109; velocity 1.26–1.27x, eddy viscosity 1.7–1.8x), the
same 1.2x by which it leads ISLA on the DrivAerML surface at every size
below full data (@sec-de-drivaerml); the two curves are parallel from 54 to
109 cars and converge above 109, where GeoTransolver's slope halves. With
the signed distance, in float32 the pressure deficit is 1.19x at 54 cars,
1.18x at 109 and 1.06x at 435, velocity moves from parity to an ISLA
advantage (0.94x at 54, 0.83x at 109, 0.73x at 435), and eddy viscosity
stays 1.3–1.5x in GeoTransolver's favour throughout; the pressure
crossover that the bfloat16 numbers showed between 109 and 435 cars does
not occur in float32 (results/v0l_reduction_2026-09-08b.json for bfloat16;
results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_interior_2026-09-09.json). The
eddy-viscosity gap, flat across an eightfold change in data with the inputs
matched, is what GeoTransolver's local features and 2.8x parameters still
buy. The ISLA-native reading of "local features", measure-weighted
surface-patch integrals at three radii around each query, was tested and
does not close it: eddy viscosity 1.36x GeoTransolver-volume in float32
(bfloat16 0.127 against 0.122 without the channel, also 1.36x; past the
preregistered 1.25 falsifier), pressure and velocity unchanged within 1%
(results/a35_v0_reduction_2026-09-08b.json). What GeoTransolver aggregates
locally is the neighbouring interior points, not the surface; that, or its
parameters, is where the last 1.27x lives. The neighbour reading was then
tested directly and does not close it either. Two flag-gated channels give
the query-token model what a local aggregation could read from the query
cloud: a scalar with the local density of queries within a ball of radius
0.05 (the count and its logarithm), and an ISLA-native channel of invariants
over each query's 16 nearest queries (distances, relative directions dotted
with the drive and the normal). In float32 on two seeds the density scalar
stands at 1.32x GeoTransolver-volume on eddy viscosity and the neighbour
channel at 1.30x, against 1.28x for the same model without either; the
preregistered bars were 1.10x to close and 1.25x to fail
(results/qtdens_reduction_2026-09-10.json, @sec-nb-qt-density-verdict).
Pressure and velocity move by less than 5%. Handing the model the sample
density outright gains nothing, so the gap is not in what the query side is
told about its own discretization at this width, and capacity is the
candidate left standing. A width increase narrows it
without closing it: the same configuration at hidden width 256 (about 15.7M
parameters) stands at 1.17x GeoTransolver-volume on eddy viscosity in
float32 (1.26x in bfloat16), inside the preregistered inconclusive band
(1.10–1.25), with pressure 4% better (1.02x GeoTransolver-volume) and
velocity 0.72x (results/a35_v0_reduction_2026-09-08c.json for bfloat16;
results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_interior_2026-09-09.json). This is a
width *increase*, not a matched width: GeoTransolver-volume's blocks run at
an effective width of 448 once its six 32-channel local features are
appended to the 256-wide token, so the null leaves capacity as a candidate
and excludes only the specific step from 192 to 256. Like every ISLA
interior arm, this one saw about 365 surface cells (@sec-interior-task).
Two further qualifications on the eddy-viscosity gap. The
metric is on the standardized viscosity (@sec-interior-task), so the 1.29x
is an ordering under that centering and not a statement about physical
viscosity error. And DrivAerML's closure is a hybrid RANS/LES model whose
modeled viscosity depends on a grid or filter length, so a query's
neighbours in the volume mesh carry information about the discretization as
well as about the flow. That GeoTransolver's local aggregation recovers
discretization information rather than a physical wall feature was the
hypothesis behind the density and neighbour channels above; their null
weakens it without ruling out a mechanism those channels do not reproduce. For the passive decode, neither
construction of a query normal closes the gap, the SDF gradient is the
better of the two by 1.2x, and the distance stratification shows the excess
error concentrated at the wall with a ratio that grows away from it
(@sec-interior-distance); a request-independent probe
set that would supply interior context while keeping the passive decode is a
design, not a result, and is not pursued while the query-token
configuration leads on two fields of three. The exact-kernel decoder is
not a contender on this task. @sec-limits collects the interior limits
alongside the book's others.
